# Resilience to a compound disturbance: sea-star wasting + marine heatwave

*Generated by `code/R/20_compound_disturbance.R`. A different-stressor-type
complement to the heat-only framing of Kumagai (2024) / our scripts 14 & 19, and to
the disease-focused Eisaguirre (2020). Brings the sea-star loss — absent from our
5-taxon harmonized data — into the picture from the raw PISCO swath.*

---

## The honest framing
In the Southern California Bight, sea-star wasting disease (SSWD, 2013–14) and the
2014–16 marine heatwave (MHW) are **temporally inseparable** — they hit in the same
three-year window. So this is a test of resilience to a **compound** stressor, not an
SSWD-specific one. What our harmonized analysis lacks, and what we add here, is the
**sea-star loss itself**, documented directly from the PISCO swath surveys.

## (A) The disease hit equally inside and outside reserves
Large sea stars (*Pycnopodia helianthoides* + *Pisaster giganteus*) crashed from
~9–11 per 60-m² transect to ~0.1 at 2013–14 and stayed there through 2022 — a
**98.8% drop outside reserves and 98.9% inside** (`table_compound_seastar_crash.csv`,
Fig. a). The crash is essentially identical inside and outside: **protection did not
buffer the sea star** (disease is not stopped by a no-take boundary). This is the
logical key — any MPA buffering of the urchin→kelp cascade after the disturbance must
come from the **protected fished predators** (spiny lobster, sheephead), not from
saving the sea star.

## (B) The cascade reorganized at the compound disturbance
Testing how the inside-vs-outside gap changed across before (≤2013) / compound
(2014–16) / after (≥2017) (`table_compound_cascade_reorg.csv`):

| Taxon | inside-vs-outside *before* | reorganization *after* |
|---|---|---|
| Spiny lobster | +0.81 (p=10⁻⁵) — already higher inside | (sustained) |
| Sheephead | +0.61 (p=10⁻⁷) — already higher inside | (sustained) |
| Purple urchin | −0.23 (ns) | **−0.88 (p=0.008)** — urchins drop inside |
| Red urchin | +0.24 (ns) | **−0.75 (p=0.002)** — urchins drop inside |
| **Giant kelp** | −0.20 (ns) — *less* kelp inside | **+1.78 (p=7×10⁻⁵)** — far *more* kelp inside |

The pattern is the compensation signature, cleanly resolved: **before** the
disturbance, reserves already held more predators (the protection effect) but *not*
fewer urchins or more kelp — because the sea star was controlling urchins everywhere,
so MPA status didn't matter for the lower cascade. **After** the sea star died
(equally inside and outside), only the MPA-protected predators remained to suppress
urchins, and the cascade reorganized: urchins fell inside reserves and **kelp flipped
from slightly lower to markedly higher inside**. The reserves' standing predator
guild became the operative urchin control exactly when the keystone predator was
removed.

## (C) Resilience holds across the compound event
On the proportion-based lnRR with the autocorrelation-robust AR1 model
(`table_compound_resilience.csv`), giant kelp is strongly more abundant inside
reserves through the compound window (compound-vs-before +1.39, p=0.0014;
after-vs-before +1.56, p=0.0002), lobster higher inside after (+0.85, p=0.005,
recovery-driven), sheephead flat, and urchin suppression in the right direction but
marginal under AR1 — consistent with scripts 14 and 19, and with the two-heatwave
replication (script 19).

## (D) Cross-study synthesis (`table_compound_crossstudy.csv`)
| Study | Region | Disturbance framing | Kelp conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eisaguirre 2020 | N. Channel Islands | SSWD (sea-star loss) | protected predators buffer kelp after sea-star loss |
| Kumagai 2024 | S. + Central CA | 2014–16 MHW | MPAs preserve cascade → kelp resilience to heat |
| **This study** | **S. California Bight** | **compound SSWD + MHW** | **kelp resilient to the compound stressor; repeats across two MHWs (script 19)** |

Three studies, three disturbance framings, one convergent conclusion — and ours is
the realistic case where the disease and the heatwave struck together.

## Caveats
- **SSWD and MHW cannot be separated** in SoCal (same window); this is a compound
  test, and we do not attribute the response to either stressor alone.
- The **structural** reorganization (kelp flip, urchin-gap widening) tied to the
  documented sea-star loss is robust, but **predator-specific attribution remains
  fragile** (sheephead–protection collinearity; see the Eisaguirre reproduction and
  the predator-diversity test) — we do not claim which protected predator does the
  compensating.
- Southern California only; urchin signals power-limited under AR1.

## Reproducibility
`code/R/20_compound_disturbance.R` (standalone; reads raw PISCO swath from the
sibling data repo for the sea-star section, skips it gracefully if absent). Outputs:
`tables/table_compound_seastar_crash.csv`, `table_compound_cascade_reorg.csv`,
`table_compound_resilience.csv`, `table_compound_crossstudy.csv`,
`plots/fig_compound_disturbance.{pdf,png}`.

### Figure legend
**Figure S — Resilience to the compound SSWD + MHW disturbance (Southern
California).** (a) Large sea-star density (*Pycnopodia* + *Pisaster*, per 60 m²) in
reserves (blue) and reference sites (orange), 2008–2022; the 2013–16 compound-
disturbance window is shaded. The ~99% crash is identical inside and outside —
protection did not buffer the disease. (b) Per-taxon MPA effect (RR = MPA /
Reference; log axis, ± 95% CI) across before / compound / after, from glmmTMB
AR1(year|MPA) + site + Source models. Giant kelp rises from below to well above
parity; urchins decline; predators stay elevated.
